records.name_note: Sources split on which common name leads, and the name two of them use is a group name. NC State's Common Name(s) list is alphabetized (Goosefoot Maple, Moosewood, Snakebark Maple, Striped Maple, Whistlewood) and runs in the same order as the page title's parenthetical, so its first entry reflects alphabetical order rather than a designated lead; NC State's Description prose opens "Snakebark maple is an understory small tree or large shrub in the maple family (Sapindaceae) with a rounded habit." MoBot's Common Name field reads "snakebark maple" (a longer Common Names list sits behind a popup whose text exists only in the link's markup, so it is not quoted here). But all three pages describe snakebark maple as a group covering more than this species: NC State's Country Or Region Of Origin field reads "Only species of snakebark maple that is native to North America", MoBot says "This is the only species of snakebark maple that is native to North America.", and RHS's description opens "A snakebark maple forming a medium-sized deciduous tree of upright growth, with white-striped green young branches." -- so that name is not used as this species' common_name. RHS's plant profile renders the H1 "Acer pensylvanicum" with the standalone subtitle "moosewood" and lists "goose foot, snake-bark maple, striped dogwood, striped maple" under Other common names. Moosewood, the only dedicated-page lead that names this species alone, is used here; Striped Maple is the species-unique name all three pages carry but none leads with. On the etymologies, NC State says "The interesting bark on stems and young trunks have white striped markings giving it the common name of snakebark. The shape of the leaves are supposedly the shape of a goosefoot giving it the common name of goosefoot maple.", and MoBot adds "Greenish bark on young branches and young trunks is vertically marked with distinctive white stripes (hence the common names of snakebark maple and striped maple)."
unknowns: No admissible source (NC State, MoBot, or RHS) carries a Poison block, a Poisonous Plant Type/Problems tag, or any cat/dog-scoped toxicity statement for Acer pensylvanicum. Red Maple's horse toxicity does not transfer to this species and no equivalent evidence for Striped Maple was found, so toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are left null rather than assumed.

outdoor_sun_exposure excludes full_sun: RHS's Position field lists 'Full sun, Partial shade', but both North American structured fields exclude it - NC State explicitly warns 'Protect it from full sun as leaves may scorch,' and MoBot's Culture prose says 'Plants dislike full sun conditions.'

outdoor_sun_exposure excludes full_shade: NC State's Light field alone tags 'Deep shade,' but MoBot's single-value Sun field reads only 'Part shade,' excluding it, so full_shade is disclosed rather than carried.

soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State's Soil pH field shows only the open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)' band (no Neutral band value given), so no closed-band ceiling/floor can be read off it; RHS's pH field lists 'Acid or Neutral' with no numeric bounds either, so no admissible source supports a numeric soil_ph_min or soil_ph_max.

water_regime left null: MoBot's structured Water field reads 'Medium,' which per rule is mid-scale and cannot support keep_moist; MoBot's Culture prose separately says 'consistently moist soils are preferred,' but this is soil-moisture cultivation language rather than an explicit watering-frequency statement, and no source frames watering as a dry-down cycle, so water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, and water_dormant_days_est are all left null.

No admissible source gives a numeric chill-damage onset temperature, day/night temperature range, humidity percentage or need rating, light in foot-candles, direct-sun hour maximum, or a fertilizing schedule/strength for this species, so those fields are left null.

cool_rest_note left null: NC State notes the species 'performs best in cooler summers so it struggles in the south' and MoBot notes 'Best performance occurs in cool summer climates,' but these are regional-climate-suitability statements, not a dormancy/cool-rest care instruction, so no cool_rest_note value was derived from them.

common_name changed at landing from 'Snakebark Maple' to 'Moosewood' on the audit's finding that snakebark maple is a group name all three pages describe as covering more than this species (see name_note); 'Striped Maple' is the species-unique fallback shared by all three pages but led by none.

is_edible left null: NC State page (the anchor) has 0 hits for 'Edible' and no statement that the plant or any part is eaten or grown for food; RHS page also has 0 hits for 'Edible'. No page addresses eating at all, so per the rules this is null, not false.
Checked NC State and RHS for 'Poison', 'Toxic', and 'Problem for' before setting is_edible -- all zero hits on both pages, so no toxicity language exists to disclose.

plantfinder.mobot.org (Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder) returned a fetch error (ConnectError) via qc.py and could not be read; this machine is refused by that host, so nothing from it is represented here and no value was guessed.

RHS gives Max Height 8-12 metres and Max Spread 'wider than 8 metres' for this species, but NC State's Plant Toolbox has its own structured Dimensions block (Height: 15 ft. 0 in. - 35 ft. 0 in.; Width: 12 ft. 0 in. - 20 ft. 0 in.), so per the anchor rule NC State's figures were used for height and spread instead of RHS's; RHS's open-ended 'wider than 8 metres' spread figure was not used for that reason (and would have given no usable upper bound in any case).

records.name_note: Sources split on which common name leads. NC State's Common Name(s) field stacks seven entries in alphabetical order — Alabama Serviceberry, Downy Serviceberry, Juneberries, Serviceberry, Service-tree, Shadblow, Shadbush — so its first entry reflects alphabetization, not a lead; its own body prose opens "Downy serviceberry, is a deciduous tree in the Rosaceae (rose) family" and uses the same name again in its cultural-conditions sentence. MoBot's displayed Common Name field reads "serviceberry" alone — a genus-umbrella term — while MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics prose calls the species "commonly called downy serviceberry." Clemson's multi-species factsheet HGIC 1026, titled "Serviceberry" and covering A. arborea alongside A. laevis, A. canadensis and A. x grandiflora cultivars in a Related Species & Cultivars section, opens on this species with "Downy serviceberry (Amelanchier arborea) is a deciduous, small tree or shrub in the rose family (Rosaceae)" and separately gives Juneberry, Shadbush and Sarvistree as regional names. UF/IFAS's dedicated single-species publication ENH232/ST073 is titled "Amelanchier arborea: Downy Serviceberry" and its Common name(s) field reads "Downy serviceberry, juneberry." RHS's page has no "Other common names" section; its heading renders "Amelanchier arborea | tree amelanchier." On the strength of UF/IFAS's dedicated-page title and Common name(s) field, and the concurring body prose at NC State, MoBot and Clemson, "Downy Serviceberry" is used as the lead common name.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail left null: none of the admissible sources checked (NC State, MoBot, RHS, Clemson, UF/IFAS) carry a toxicity/poison statement for Amelanchier arborea. NC State's page for this species has no Poison Part/Poison Severity field and no 'Poisonous' Plant Type or Problems tag, so there is no Poison block to capture.
humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max left null: no admissible source addresses ambient humidity for this outdoor landscape tree.
day_f_min/max and night_f_min/max left null: no admissible source frames indoor/outdoor temperature thresholds for this field-grown tree.

chill_damage_f left null: NC State gives only a USDA Plant Hardiness Zone range (4a through 9b), which is a zone/survival rating, not a stated damage-onset temperature, so per the rules it cannot be used to fill this field.

light_fc_min, light_fc_good, and direct_sun_hours_max left null: no admissible source states a foot-candle figure or a species-specific maximum direct-sun-hours figure; NC State's 'Full sun (6 or more hours...)' text is the site-wide light-category legend, not species-specific prose, so it was not used.

outdoor_sun_exposure excludes 'part_sun': UF/IFAS's Light requirement field additionally lists 'partial sun or partial shade, full sun,' but neither of the two North American structured fields used as primary (NC State's Light field: Full sun, Partial Shade; MoBot's Sun field: Full sun to part shade) carries a part_sun value, so per the rules that UF/IFAS value is disclosed here rather than carried into the list.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max derivation: NC State's Soil pH field carries only the open-ended bands Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), so no closed numeric range could be derived from it. The 5.5-7.0 figures come from Clemson HGIC 1026. RHS's page does carry a pH field, reading "Acid or Neutral"; it excludes Alkaline and so corroborates rather than contradicts the Clemson range, as does RHS's cultivation instruction to use lime-free soil.

water_regime left null: no admissible source frames watering for this species as a checked wet/dry cadence. MoBot's structured Water field reads 'Water: Medium,' a mid-scale value that per the rules cannot support keep_moist; it is noted here only as a disclosed data point, not used to set the field.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis left null: this is an in-ground landscape tree/shrub and no source frames watering in check-and-water or day-interval terms.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength left null: no admissible source gives a fertilizing schedule or dilution strength specific to this species; UF/IFAS mentions 'regular fertilization' only in passing, as a way to reduce borer susceptibility, not as a schedule.

NC State's page notes the species is 'commonly sold in the nursery trade as Amelanchier canadensis, although canadensis is, in fact, a shrubby East Coast species' -- a taxonomic-confusion note relevant to distinguishing this entry from the catalog's existing Amelanchier canadensis entry, included here for awareness rather than as a formal name_note sub-claim since the A. canadensis page itself was not re-fetched in this session.

soil_base 'garden_bed' is inferred from the species being described throughout the admissible sources as an in-ground landscape/woodland tree grown in ordinary soil textures (clay, loam, sand), not from any source using that literal token.

No poisonous-part, toxicity, or 'problem for' language was found on the NC State anchor page (searched 'Poison', 'Toxic', 'Problem for' via qc.py: 0 hits each), so is_edible=true carries no toxicity caveat to disclose from this source.

Only the NC State Plant Toolbox page was needed to source all six fields with high confidence; RHS, Missouri Botanical Garden, Clemson HGIC, and UF/IFAS pages were not queried since the anchor already supplied structured Dimensions, Attracts, and Edibility fields with no gaps or conflicts to resolve.

mature_height_in and mature_spread_in reflect only the cultivated-landscape range NC State gives (15-25 ft height, 10-15 ft width); the same page separately notes wild specimens can reach 40 ft, but that figure is not a published min/max bound so it is not recorded in the range fields.

is_edible removed on audit: The null rests on a factually false unknowns entry. The unknowns claim "none of the three assigned pages ... address eating this plant or any part of it ... found no statement of food use." The NC State page (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/tsuga-canadensis/) carries a structured "Uses (Ethnobotany):" field reading, verbatim: "The cambium is used by Native Americans for breads and soups as well as with dried fruit and animal fat for pemmican. The leaves, which are high in vitamin C, are also used for tea." The search strategy failed, not the page -- the word "Edible" genuinely has 0 hits on NC State and RHS (I confirmed both), but NC State files food use under "Uses (Ethnobotany)", never under "Edible". Two named human food uses of two named parts (cambium, leaves) is not silence. The field must be re-decided against that text, and if it lands on true the preparation conditions in that text (cambium cooked into breads/soups, leaves steeped as tea -- not raw whole-plant eating) must appear in unknowns. Separately, the toxicity half of the disclosure is accurate: "Poison", "poisonous" and "irritant" all return 0 hits on both accessible pages, and NC State's 6 "Toxic" hits are only the tag strings "#non-toxic for cats", "#non-toxic for horses", "#non-toxic for dogs".
